    Generating outliers¶

    Outliers are appended data points: the generator samples new rows that look extreme relative to the given data, and stacks them after the original rows — so Xt is larger than X. Use outliers to test how pipelines behave when rare, extreme observations appear: robust statistics, anomaly detection, scaling, and model fitting all react very differently to them.

    This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

    1. Acting on the observation process — sample outliers directly from a distribution fitted to the data: one generic OutlierSamplingGenerator plus a pluggable out-of-distribution sampler (z-score, hypersphere, histogram and low-density). This generator does not use a DGP.
    2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — perturb a node of a fitted causal model; the perturbation propagates to the descendants, so the outliers are not just extreme — they are structurally consistent extreme events (CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator).

    Labels: the generated rows are the last rows appended to Xt (the count is set by the selector's count); the boolean array is exposed via get_outliers_labels().

    Goal¶

    Generate out-of-distribution points in tabular data — sampled directly from the data's own geometry (Part A) or propagated along a causal graph (Part B) — and identify which rows are outliers.

    In [1]:
    Copied!

    def plot_outliers(X, Xt, labels, cls=None):
    """
    Plot original data and the transformed data (outliers marked).
    labels = boolean outlier labels (get_outliers_labels());
    cls = optional class vector for coloring the original data.
    """
    outliers = Xt[labels]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharex=True, sharey=True, figsize=(8,4))
    if cls is not None:
        for i in range(len(np.unique(cls))):
            ix = np.where(cls == i)
            axes[0].scatter(X[ix,0],X[ix,1], c = f'C{i}', label = f'{i}')
            axes[1].scatter(X[ix,0],X[ix,1], c = f'C{i}', label = f'{i}')
    else:
        axes[0].scatter(X[:,0], X[:,1], c='C0', label='original')
        axes[1].scatter(X[:,0], X[:,1], c='C0', label='original')
    axes[1].scatter(outliers[:,0],outliers[:,1], marker = 'x', c = f'black', label = 'outliers')
    axes[0].set_title('Original')
    axes[1].set_title('Transformed')
    axes[1].legend(ncol=1, bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig, axes

    Load and prepare data¶

    We first load an existing dataset from sklearn.datasets.

    Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶

    OutlierSamplingGenerator samples outlier rows from a distribution or density derived directly from the data — the strategy is chosen by the out-of-distribution sampler passed to generate() (a registry name or a sampler instance from badgers.core.sampling). No causal model is involved; the outliers are marginal extremes, unrelated to any structure between the columns. The required CountSelector owns the count of appended rows (count) and the columns to perturb.

    Generate outliers using z-score sampling¶

    The "zscore" sampler (ZScoreSampler) generates points whose z-score (distance to the mean, in units of the standard deviation) exceeds 3 — far out on the tails of the empirical distribution.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")
labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()
print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore") labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    appending: (100, 2) -> (125, 2) | outlier rows: 25

    Generate outliers using hypersphere sampling¶

    The "hypersphere" sampler (HypersphereSampler) generates points uniformly on a hypersphere (a shell around the data) — extreme in every direction, not only along single axes.

    Generate outliers using independent histogram sampling¶

    The "independent_histogram" sampler (IndependentHistogramSampler) fits a histogram to each column independently, then samples outliers from the empty (or rare) bins — combinations that never occur in the data.

    Generate outliers using histogram sampling¶

    The "histogram" sampler (JointHistogramSampler) works on the joint histogram of the data — but only for low-dimensional datasets (the bin count explodes with dimensionality).

    Generate outliers using low density sampling¶

    The "low_density" sampler (KernelDensitySampler) samples points in the low-density regions of the empirical distribution — between and beyond the clusters, rather than at the extremes of single columns. It is a grid-CDF construction with no rejection step: a bounded regular grid (sized by grid_budget) is scored once with a kernel density estimate, and points are drawn from a categorical over the low-density grid cells — the generator always appends exactly selector.count points, deterministically for a fixed seed.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler=KernelDensitySampler(
                      threshold_low_density=0.1, grid_budget=256))
labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()
print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler=KernelDensitySampler( threshold_low_density=0.1, grid_budget=256)) labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum())) 
    appending: (100, 2) -> (125, 2) | outlier rows: 25

    Generate outliers using tree sampling¶

    The "tree" sampler (TreeCellSampler) is an adaptive histogram — no kernel density estimate: recursive median splits partition the data into cells holding at most leaf_size points, so the resolution is fine in dense regions and coarse in sparse ones. Every cell is extended axis-aligned across the full gap to the nearest data point on each side (the outermost cells reach the data-box boundary), so the leaves tile the whole box; a bounded coverage grid then finds every box region not covered by any leaf and adds it as an always-qualifying empty cell, so the space around and between the clusters is reachable as well. Points are drawn from a categorical over the cells whose extended-territory density is at most threshold_low_density times the global mean density, weighted by cell volume — the generator always appends exactly selector.count points.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler=TreeCellSampler(
                      threshold_low_density=0.1))
labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()
print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler=TreeCellSampler( threshold_low_density=0.1)) labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() print('appending:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))

    Generate outliers in a reduced space (decomposition + sampling)¶

    For higher-dimensional data, a first step is to reduce the dimensionality (any sklearn transformer with transform/inverse_transform, e.g. PCA, KernelPCA, FastICA) and sample outliers in the reduced space: StructuredOutlierGenerator chains a decomposition and an outlier sampler — outliers are sampled where the data really has little support, in the informative subspace rather than the noisy one.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA

# generate some data with higher dimensionality
X_hi, y_hi = make_blobs(n_features=10, centers=4, cluster_std=0.5, random_state=0)
cls_hi = y_hi.astype(int)

gen = StructuredOutlierGenerator(
    dimension_reduction_transformer=PCA(n_components=3),
    outlier_generator=OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng),
)
Xt = gen.generate(X_hi.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")
labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()
print('appending:', X_hi.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA # generate some data with higher dimensionality X_hi, y_hi = make_blobs(n_features=10, centers=4, cluster_std=0.5, random_state=0) cls_hi = y_hi.astype(int) gen = StructuredOutlierGenerator( dimension_reduction_transformer=PCA(n_components=3), outlier_generator=OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng), ) Xt = gen.generate(X_hi.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore") labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() print('appending:', X_hi.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))

    Preprocessing stays out of the generator's responsibility: instead of the built-in standardization + decomposition, a custom transformer can be passed as preprocessor (anything with transform/inverse_transform, e.g. a fitted sklearn pipeline):

    In [20]:
    Copied! 
    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA

gen = StructuredOutlierGenerator(
    outlier_generator=OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng),
    preprocessor=make_pipeline(RobustScaler(), FastICA(n_components=3, whiten="unit-variance")),
)
Xt = gen.generate(X_hi.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")
labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()
print('appending:', X_hi.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA gen = StructuredOutlierGenerator( outlier_generator=OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=rng), preprocessor=make_pipeline(RobustScaler(), FastICA(n_components=3, whiten="unit-variance")), ) Xt = gen.generate(X_hi.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=25, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore") labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() print('appending:', X_hi.shape, '->', Xt.shape, '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))

    Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶

    CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator perturbs a node of a fitted causal model with do()-style intervention: the node is set to an extreme value and the descendants are recomputed through the structural equations. The result: outliers that are extreme and structurally consistent — unlike Part A's marginal extremes, these respect the relationships between the columns.

    The choice of perturbed node matters, and the topology decides how far the effect reaches — that is what the following examples show.

    In [22]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import badgers
badgers.__version__

    Out[22]:
    '0.1.0'
    In [23]:
    Copied! 
    # ============================================================
# Helper functions for the topology examples
# ============================================================

def generate_linear_data(graph, n_samples=100, rng=None, coefficients=None):
    """Generate data from a linear structural equation model defined by a DAG.

    Each edge (u -> v) has a coefficient w_uv. Node values are computed as:
        v = sum_{u in parents(v)} w_uv * u + noise
    where noise ~ N(0, 1).

    Parameters
    ----------
    graph : nx.DiGraph
        The causal DAG. Node names must be strings.
    n_samples : int
        Number of samples to generate.
    rng : np.random.Generator, optional
        Random number gen.
    coefficients : dict, optional
        Edge coefficients. Defaults to 1.0 for all edges.

    Returns
    -------
    X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_nodes)
    column_mapping : dict[str, int]
    """
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    if coefficients is None:
        coefficients = {edge: 1.0 for edge in graph.edges()}

    nodes = list(graph.nodes())
    node_to_idx = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)}
    n_nodes = len(nodes)

    X = np.zeros((n_samples, n_nodes))
    topo_order = list(nx.topological_sort(graph))

    for node in topo_order:
        idx = node_to_idx[node]
        parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
        if not parents:
            # Exogenous node: pure noise
            X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples)
        else:
            # Endogenous node: weighted sum of parents + noise
            X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples)
            for parent in parents:
                parent_idx = node_to_idx[parent]
                coef = coefficients.get((parent, node), 1.0)
                X[:, idx] += coef * X[:, parent_idx]

    column_mapping = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)}
    return X, column_mapping
    # ============================================================ # Helper functions for the topology examples # ============================================================ def generate_linear_data(graph, n_samples=100, rng=None, coefficients=None): """Generate data from a linear structural equation model defined by a DAG. Each edge (u -> v) has a coefficient w_uv. Node values are computed as: v = sum_{u in parents(v)} w_uv * u + noise where noise ~ N(0, 1). Parameters ---------- graph : nx.DiGraph The causal DAG. Node names must be strings. n_samples : int Number of samples to generate. rng : np.random.Generator, optional Random number gen. coefficients : dict, optional Edge coefficients. Defaults to 1.0 for all edges. Returns ------- X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_nodes) column_mapping : dict[str, int] """ if rng is None: rng = np.random.default_rng(42) if coefficients is None: coefficients = {edge: 1.0 for edge in graph.edges()} nodes = list(graph.nodes()) node_to_idx = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)} n_nodes = len(nodes) X = np.zeros((n_samples, n_nodes)) topo_order = list(nx.topological_sort(graph)) for node in topo_order: idx = node_to_idx[node] parents = list(graph.predecessors(node)) if not parents: # Exogenous node: pure noise X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples) else: # Endogenous node: weighted sum of parents + noise X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples) for parent in parents: parent_idx = node_to_idx[parent] coef = coefficients.get((parent, node), 1.0) X[:, idx] += coef * X[:, parent_idx] column_mapping = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)} return X, column_mapping

    def plot_data(X, labels, column_names):
    """Scatter-matrix of the data with outliers highlighted in red.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
    labels : array-like or None
        Labels: "original" or "outliers". If None, all points are "original".
    column_names : list of str
        Names for each column.
    """
    is_outlier = np.asarray(labels) == "outliers" if labels is not None else np.zeros(len(X), dtype=bool)
    d = len(column_names)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(d, d, figsize=(2.5 * d, 2.5 * d))
    for i in range(d):
        for j in range(d):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            if i == j:
                # diagonal: histogram of the original data
                ax.hist(X[~is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C0", alpha=0.7)
                if is_outlier.any():
                    ax.hist(X[is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C3", alpha=0.7)
                ax.set_ylabel("Count") if j == 0 else ax.set_yticklabels([])
            elif i > j:
                ax.set_visible(False)  # hide lower triangle
            else:
                # upper triangle: scatter + regression line on original data
                ax.scatter(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], color="C0", s=15, alpha=0.6)
                ax.scatter(X[is_outlier, j], X[is_outlier, i], color="C3", s=30, alpha=0.6)
                if (~is_outlier).sum() > 1:
                    coef = np.polyfit(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], 1)
                    xs = np.array([X[~is_outlier, j].min(), X[~is_outlier, j].max()])
                    ax.plot(xs, coef[0] * xs + coef[1], color="C0", linewidth=1, alpha=0.5)
            if i == d - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel(column_names[j])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(column_names[i])
    fig.suptitle("Data scatter-matrix (red = outliers)", y=1.02, fontsize=13)
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig

    def draw_graph(graph, title=None):
    """Draw a DAG with fixed left-to-right node positions.

    Nodes are placed in topological generations: roots at x = 0, their
    descendants at x = 1, and so on; siblings are stacked vertically.
    This keeps the visual layout deterministic and consistent across
    all notebooks (no force-directed layout).
    """
    generations = {}  # node -> column index
    for node in nx.topological_sort(graph):
        parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
        generations[node] = 0 if not parents else max(generations[p] for p in parents) + 1
    columns = {}
    pos = {}
    for node, col in generations.items():
        pos[node] = (col, columns.setdefault(col, 0))
        columns[col] += 1
    # center each column vertically
    height = max(columns.values())
    pos = {node: (x, y - (columns[x] - 1) / 2) for node, (x, y) in pos.items()}
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 2))
    nx.draw(graph, pos, ax=ax, node_color="lightblue", node_size=800, arrowsize=15)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(graph, pos, ax=ax)
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.axis("off")
    return fig

    Chain: \(X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z\)¶

    Perturbing X affects Y (direct child) and Z (indirect child). Perturbing Y affects Z but not X. The propagation direction is always downstream.

X_chain, mapping_chain = generate_linear_data(chain, n_samples=100, rng=rng, coefficients=coefs_chain)

print(f"X_chain shape: {X_chain.shape}")

    import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.causal import CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

    Sampling strategy comparison¶
    The within_distribution_sampler and out_of_distribution_sampler
parameters control how the outlier values are drawn at the perturbation
node:
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [38]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    from badgers.core.sampling import (
    create_out_of_distribution_sampler,
    UniformOutOfDistributionSampler,
)

# Use the chain graph from section 6.1
sampler_configs = [
    ("zscore", {}),
    ("hypersphere", {}),
    ("uniform", {"expansion": 0.5}),
]
n_outliers = 20

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, (sampler_name, kwargs) in zip(axes, sampler_configs):
    if kwargs:
        sampler = create_out_of_distribution_sampler(sampler_name, **kwargs)
    else:
        sampler = sampler_name

    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(make_scm(chain), mapping_chain).fit(X_chain)
    gen = CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator(random_generator=rng, dgp=dgp)
    Xt = gen.generate(
        X_chain.copy(),
        selector=CountSelector([0], count=n_outliers, rng=np.random.default_rng(0)),
        out_of_distribution_sampler=sampler,
    )
    outliers = Xt[-n_outliers:]
    original = Xt[:-n_outliers]

    # Scatter: X vs Y, color by original/outlier
    ax.scatter(original[:, 0], original[:, 1], alpha=0.4, s=20, label="original", c="C0")
    ax.scatter(outliers[:, 0], outliers[:, 1], alpha=0.8, s=40, label="outliers", c="C3", edgecolors="black")
    ax.set_xlabel("X")
    ax.set_ylabel("Y")
    label = sampler_name
    if kwargs:
        label = f"{sampler_name} ({', '.join(f'{k}={v}' for k, v in kwargs.items())})"
    ax.set_title(f'out_of_distribution_sampler="{label}"')
    ax.legend()
    ax.axhline(y=0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)
    ax.axvline(x=0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)

plt.suptitle("Out-of-Distribution Sampler Comparison: X → Y (Chain Topology)", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    if kwargs:
        label = f"{sampler_name} ({', '.join(f'{k}={v}' for k, v in kwargs.items())})"
    ax.set_title(f'out_of_distribution_sampler="{label}"')
    ax.legend()
    ax.axhline(y=0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)
    ax.axvline(x=0, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)

plt.suptitle("Out-of-Distribution Sampler Comparison: X → Y (Chain Topology)", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    Key observations:
    

      

    • "zscore" (default): Outliers are pushed far from the mean (\(\geq 3\sigma\)), creating extreme but causally-consistent anomalies.
      • 

    • "hypersphere": Outliers form a spherical shell in standardized space, useful for testing detectors against uniformly-directional anomalies.
      • 

    • "uniform": Outliers spread uniformly beyond the observed range, producing diverse patterns across the full expanded space.
      • 

    

    The within-distribution sampler (default "normal") controls how exogenous
ancestor nodes are sampled — these stay within the observed distribution since
they are not directly perturbed.

    • Outliers are an appending deficit: Xt is larger than X, and the
generated rows are the last rows (one per selected seed row).
      • 

    • Outlier labels come from get_outliers_labels().
      • 

    • Part A's outliers are marginal extremes; Part B's outliers are
structurally consistent extreme events whose footprint depends on
the causal topology (chain / fork / collider / diamond).
      • 

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Takeaways¶
      

    • Outlier generators add rows beyond the data's distribution; the output has MORE rows than the input.
      • 

    • generate(X, **params) returns the single generated object Xt; the outlier flags come from gen.get_outliers_labels().
      • 

    • The causal variant (CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator) injects outliers at graph nodes and propagates them to descendants (Pearl surgery).
      •
